messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malia, a 56-year-old Oceania-born social ministry worker, had built her life around being dependable in other people’s crises, the kind of woman who stayed late after community visits, carried spare supplies in her car, and knew how to calm frightened families with a steady voice. The sexual assault that changed that happened years ago, after an evening outreach event when she was left alone with a man she knew through the congregation and social circles around her work. What had felt like a familiar, safe relationship shifted without warning into violation, and afterward she was left with the awful conviction that someone else would have stopped it, that she should have seen it coming, and that there was something fundamentally wrong with her for it to have happened at all. Once she had concluded that she could not trust her own judgment and that danger could arrive through familiar faces, ordinary days began to feel mined for warning signs; a tone of voice, a man lingering too long in her periphery, or footsteps behind her could suddenly snag her attention as proof that another violation might be close. In the weeks that followed, she noticed that even small reminders could set her body off. Seeing related people—men connected to the same circles, or anyone who resembled him in manner or tone—made her immediately tense and watchful, and she began arranging herself so she could stay close to an exit in meetings, in church halls, and even in the waiting rooms where her ministry took her. Living at that pitch of alertness made the world feel dense with threats, and the very cues she scanned for seemed to multiply around her; a door left ajar, a car idling too long outside the social ministry office, or an unexpected figure entering a room could all register as fresh reminders of what she already feared. At work, she started choosing seats by the door and scanning windows and locks before she could settle, as if every room had to be assessed for how quickly she could get out.

Her memories of the assault were not hazy but exacting. Malia described them as a film that played over and over, with details she wished she could erase: the light in the room, the sound of his voice, the feel of the furniture against her hands, the way her mind seemed to freeze while her body registered danger. The memory could force its way in when she least wanted it, and when it did she would become visibly uneasy, breathing shallowly and going rigid, as though she were back in that moment. Because she had spent so long trying to keep the assault at a distance—pushing it away, refusing to dwell on it, and bracing against anything that might bring it up—the memory seemed to stay intact and waiting, so that when it finally broke through it came back with a sharpness that startled her. Those intrusions made her feel less in control of herself, and she came to treat any discomfort—any sense of being trapped, watched, or unsettled—as a sign that danger might be near. That was one reason she kept herself near exits and repeatedly checked doors and windows in her office and at home; it was also why she covered her face with heavy makeup before public-facing ministry visits, wanting no one to see how strained and frightened she felt beneath the composed surface. Yet these efforts did not calm her for long. The more she checked, the more she noticed what could go wrong, and the more her body stayed braced for it. She was constantly tense, superalert, and easily startled by ordinary movements in hallways or by a familiar person entering a room unexpectedly.

Malia’s belief that she was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined her had slowly narrowed her life. She had once been confident moving freely between homes, hospitals, and community centers, but now she needed to plan every outing around escape routes and safety checks, and the strain of holding herself together left her exhausted. Eating excessively became one of the few ways she could blunt the surge of distress after a triggering encounter or after an intrusion had left her shaking; she would tell herself that a full stomach made the fear feel less sharp, though the relief never lasted. At other times she overused makeup in the hope that it would help her look untroubled enough to keep working. Both habits gave her a sense of control in the moment, but they also kept the assault close: the more she arranged her days around managing terror, the more alert she became to signs of danger, and the more readily ordinary experiences were linked back to what had happened. Feeling happy or relaxed had become especially uneasy for her, because when she let herself soften, the memory seemed to break in more easily, and a pleasant conversation or an easy afternoon at home could suddenly turn into a reminder of how vulnerable she had been. Over time, she began to avoid the very situations that might have restored her confidence, and the loss of that confidence reinforced her sense that she had indeed been changed in a damaging way.

By the time she sought help, Malia was no longer able to dismiss the pattern. She was still working, still married, still showing up for the people who depended on her, but only by keeping herself on guard, checking locks, staying near exits, and bracing against the sudden return of the film-like memory. She feared that if she stopped managing every detail, something would happen again, and she was frightened by how much smaller her world had become. What brought her in was the growing sense that she could not keep serving others while living as if danger were waiting around every familiar face and every closed door. More than anything, she wanted to feel capable again, and to believe that the assault had not permanently made her defective.
